title: How Afrofuturism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Afrofuturism, a movement in speculative fiction, music, art, film and comics that imagines futures and alternate histories through a Black lens. They trace precursors such as Martin Delany's 1857 novel Blake, Edward Johnson's 1901 Light Ahead for the Negro, and George Schuyler's Black No More; cover the 1993 coining of the term by Mark Dery in "Black to the Future"; discuss gatekeeping by editor John W. Campbell and the role of Samuel R. Delany, Octavia Butler and Sun Ra; and survey George Clinton and Parliament-Funkadelic, Basquiat, Janelle Monáe, Missy Elliott, Black Panther, Jordan Peele, and debates over terms like Africanfuturism and Astro-Blackness. Episode ends with listener mail about brown fat.
topics: Mark Dery Black to the Future

segments.title: Tour dates promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote the remaining 2023 tour dates and ticket links.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and say Afrofuturism is too broad to cover fully in one episode.

segments.title: Defining Afrofuturism
segments.summary: Josh defines Afrofuturism as visions of the future, fantasy and alternate realities under speculative fiction through an African American lens. They note its roots in science fiction and how sci fi has underserved Black protagonists, citing a 2016 Vox statistic that 8 percent of top grossing sci fi films featured Black protagonists.

segments.title: Early Black sci fi writers and alternate histories
segments.summary: Samuel R. Delany is described as an early Black sci fi writer in the 1960s. Martin Delany's 1857 novel Blake or the Huts of America and Edward Johnson's 1901 Light Ahead for the Negro are cited as early alternate histories by Black authors, produced without a movement behind them.
topics: Blake or the Huts of America

segments.title: Pulp magazines and gatekeeping
segments.summary: Pulp writers often used pseudonyms, which may have hidden Black and women writers. John W. Campbell, editor of Astounding Science Fiction, is described as a gatekeeper who kept sci fi white and whose essays supported segregation.

segments.title: Octavia Butler and exclusion from science fiction
segments.summary: Octavia Butler's 1980 essay The Lost Races of Science Fiction is discussed, including her critique that violence was acceptable in sci fi but race was considered too heavy. Janet Ing's criticism of Campbell's influence is also mentioned.
topics: The Lost Races of Science Fiction

segments.title: Mark Dery coins the term
segments.summary: Mark Dery coined Afrofuturism in his 1993 essay Black to the Future, interviewing Delany, Greg Tate and Tricia Rose. Dery defined it as speculative fiction treating African American themes in the context of twentieth century technoculture.

segments.title: Debate over scope: African American vs. global Black culture
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Afrofuturism should be limited to African Americans or include the African continent and the wider diaspora.

segments.title: Self-liberation and reimagining the future
segments.summary: Afrofuturist works are described as a method of self-healing and hope, and as reimagining the future through a Black lens rather than placing Black characters in a white-coded future, with the idea of defamiliarizing the future.

segments.title: George Schuyler and Black No More
segments.summary: George Schuyler, a conservative writer who also wrote pulp stories under the pseudonym Samuel I. Brooks, is described as an early progenitor. Black No More imagines a machine that turns Black people white.

segments.title: Sun Ra
segments.summary: Sun Ra, born Herman Blount in Birmingham in 1914, moved to Chicago and then New York and developed an experimental jazz orchestra with a Saturn mythos. His 1957 album Supersonic Jazz is recommended as an accessible starting point.

segments.title: George Clinton and Parliament-Funkadelic
segments.summary: George Clinton and the mothership stage show are discussed, including a replica at the National Museum of African American History in DC, which hosts an Afrofuturism exhibit. The hosts describe Parliament's afronaut mythos as bringing a fractured Black community together after the MLK assassination.
topics: National Museum of African American History

segments.title: Lonnie Holly and Lee Scratch Perry
segments.summary: Chuck recommends Atlanta musician Lonnie Holly as a modern example of the aesthetic. Josh mentions Lee Scratch Perry and dub reggae as sometimes cited Afrofuturist.

segments.title: Visual art: Basquiat, Rammellzee and Octavia Butler's career
segments.summary: Jean-Michel Basquiat is named as an early Afrofuturist in fine art influenced by funk and hip hop. Rammellzee is described as a graffiti artist, sculptor and performer. Octavia Butler's career and the biography The Spectacular Life of Octavia Butler are discussed.

segments.title: Octavia Butler's works and Kindred adaptation
segments.summary: Kindred is mentioned along with a TV adaptation that FX canceled after one season. Parable of the Sower and the Xenogenesis series are also noted.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Mainstream film: Will Smith, Jordan Peele and Colson Whitehead
segments.summary: Afrofuturism is said to have become mainstream from the late 1990s, with Will Smith's sci fi roles cited as a breakthrough. Jordan Peele's Nope and Colson Whitehead's novels are described as having Afrofuturist elements.

segments.title: Afrofuturism in hip hop, Missy Elliott, Digable Planets and comics
segments.summary: Hip hop is described as carrying Afrofuturist DNA, citing Cool Keith's Doctor Octagon, Wu-Tang and Ol' Dirty Bastard's Bobby Digital, Beyoncé, Janelle Monáe, Missy Elliott, and Digable Planets. Black Kirby (John Jennings and Stacy Robinson) and Ebon are discussed, along with Major Sankofa.

segments.title: Black Panther and African accents
segments.summary: Black Panther is cited as a mainstream Afrofuturist film. Chadwick Boseman is credited with insisting the African characters use South African accents rather than British ones.

segments.title: Terminology debates and current state
segments.summary: Tochi Anyanwu's view that Afrofuturism must address Black suffering is mentioned. Alternative terms such as Astro-Blackness, Ethnogothic, Black fantastic, magical realism, and Africanfuturism (Nnedi Okorafor) are presented. The hosts argue Afrofuturism has become mainstream and includes artists such as Manuel Bowman, Lina Iris Victor, Kamasi Washington and Janelle Monáe.

segments.title: Closing discussion and Janelle Monáe
segments.summary: Janelle Monáe's Dirty Computer and Memory Library are praised. The hosts discuss upcoming concerts, including Beyoncé and Taylor Swift, before moving to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: brown fat
segments.summary: Listener Sarah Batton writes about brown fat's role in releasing heat and in cold adaptation, following the intermittent fasting episode, and announces her chemical engineering degree.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard closing and production credit.
